newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Euro shares cut losses, Wall St/dlr steady.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Euro shares cut losses, Wall St/dlr steady.

text.p: European stock markets defied fears of a major slide to curb their losses on Monday, while Wall Street made a hesitant recovery from its second biggest points fall in history.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which had lost 247.37 points or more than three percent on Friday, showed only a fractional net change as European trading ended for the day.

"There was just a sense of disappointment that the market could not hold in and there is a little bit of nervousness about tomorrow's Fed meeting," said Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co in New York as the Dow ran out of steam after an early rally.
The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meets to consider interest rates on Tuesday but is not generally expected by economists to raise them just yet.

European investors had looked to Wall Street for tips on what to do next amid uncertainty on whether Friday's drop marked an end to a relentless rise in U.S. and European share prices or just a short-term correction.

"We see this as another periodic bout of profit-taking nervousness...There is some froth there to be taken out but nothing fundamental has changed," said Tony Robinson, head of equities at fund manager Lombard Odier.

"Some people feared that Friday was the start of something bigger but there are striking differences between what happened Friday and the crash of 1987. Bond markets are resilient, the liquidity is there and corporations are handing cash back," BZW strategist Steve Wright in London said.
Steadier stock markets rubbed off on the dollar, which ended with little net change. It earlier suffered jitters over the possibility of higher German interest rates.
But gold lost earlier moderate gains and dealers said investors still seemed to lack trust in precious metals as safe financial havens.

After Friday's loss, the Dow, the barometer of U.S. blue-chip shares, had fallen 6.8 percent from a record close of 8,259.31 on August 6. But it was still more than 3,000 points or nearly 66 percent above its level two years ago.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average in Tokyo, taking its cue from the Dow, fell 1.47 percent on Monday.

Continental European markets, several closed on Friday for a holiday, were then generally hit more than London, Europe's largest stock market, which had already responded to the early stages of Friday's Dow plunge.
London's FTSE index had tumbled 125.5 points or 2.5 percent on Friday but this compared with a much larger plunge of 250.7 points, or 12.22 percent, in the "crash" of October 20, 1987.
Having opened on Monday with a loss of nearly 1.5 percent, the FTSE ended around 0.6 percent lower, aided by higher bond prices and investors seeking bargains.

In Frankfurt floor trade the DAX index showed an early fall of some four percent but it had closed on Friday before Wall Street's retreat. It finally more than halved its loss and the IBIS index rose further in late electronic business.
"We have to remember that the DAX has been a real performer this year and it was time for some sort of a correction," said a Frankfurt dealer.

Paris, one of a number of markets closed on Friday for Assumption Day, was particularly hard hit with the CAC-40 down some 3.3 percent at one stage before ending with a loss of 1.77 percent, aided by a revival in the dollar.
"Technically the market remains well-oriented. There was a sell-off at the opening due to Wall Street but there never was any panic," said one Paris broker.

In contrast, the Amsterdam bourse moved well into the plus column after early losses, gaining 2.6 percent. "We were the most negative, so it's not a great surprise to see us as the most positive today," one Dutch trader said.
The dollar rose back above 1.82 marks after being hit by jitters on higher German rates before the Bundesbank's first meeting after the summer break on Thursday.
"Fears of knock-on effect today from Friday's (Wall Street) sell-off seem to have been overdone," said Sanjit Maitra, head of economics and strategy at WestLB in London.

Economists doubt whether the German central bank would move towards higher interest rates at Tuesday's repo tender or tighten credit after Thursday's council meeting since remarks showing German officials' concern about the mark's decline and inflation have already made an impact.

"Now that there seems to be some calming down of those pressures (mark weaknesss), I think the Bundesbank is happy not to do anything," Deutsche Bank chief economist Norbert Walter told Reuters Financial Television.
The dollar/yen rate pushed higher again but stayed below 118 yen. It had been capped by remarks from U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang who expressed concern about Japanese trade data.

Analysts, meanwhile, said gold's retreat to 12-year lows this year had taken the shine off the former "safe haven" for investors. "They are very wary of gold. It's been a dreadful investment," said analyst Ted Arnold of Merrill Lynch.
CURRENCIES AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar was quoted around 1.8220 marks and 117.76 yen versus 1.8227 and 117.76 in late European trading on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT THE EUROPEAN CLOSE
LONDON - The FTSE 100 index closed down 30.8 points or 0.63 percent at 4,835.0.
FRANKFURT - The DAX index ended floor trade 74.26 points, 1.79 percent, lower at 4,078.60. The IBIS index for electronic trade finished up 2.96 points, 0.07 percent, at 4,080.55.
PARIS - The CAC-40 index ended 51.71 points or 1.77 percent lower at 2,870.13.
The Madrid stock market lost 2.3 percent, Milan 2.1 percent, Stockholm 0.7 percent and Zurich 1.7 percent. The Amsterdam bourse was up 2.6 percent.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold ended London trading around $323.25/ounce, up from its afternoon fix of $322.60 but below a morning fix of $326.05 and Friday's close of $324.35. Silver gained seven cents to $4.52.
